metadata.file_name: 73. Yun et al. (2025). Discovering action insights from large-scale assessment log data using machine learning.pdf
metadata.title: Discovering action insights from large-scale assessment log data using machine learning

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses the 2012 PIAAC log dataset for two problem sets (“Party Invitation” and “Club Membership”) and constructs analytic samples by filtering out incomplete logs or sequences with missing actions. The manuscript reports stratification by performance levels for comparisons and then builds sequence embeddings (Word2Vec/Doc2Vec) followed by supervised group classification (neural network and random forest). No complex survey weighting variables (e.g., W_FSTUWT/TOTWGT) or replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife) are mentioned, and the ML models are trained on behavioral action-sequence representations rather than PV-based achievement scores. Given the absence of explicit weighting discussion, the analysis should be treated as unweighted with respect to PIAAC’s complex survey design, which may limit population-representativeness of the classification results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The dependent variables are performance groups derived from PIAAC problem-set scores (e.g., score0 vs score3; correct vs incorrect) based on action-sequence logs, not PV-based cognitive achievement scales. The paper states that incomplete logs/sequences with missing actions were removed during preprocessing, but it does not provide a formal missing-data handling method for other variables used in modeling (e.g., whether any additional missingness was imputed or how remaining missingness was treated). This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling beyond the explicit log-completeness filter.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used the 2012 PIAAC log data for two specific problem sets: “Party Invitation” (35 distinct actions) and “Club Membership” (25 distinct actions). Preprocessed the dataset to remove incomplete logs or sequences with missing actions, then stratified by performance levels to compare high- vs low-performing groups. For feature verification, created three cases per problem set by using (case1) all actions, (case2) only the identified meaningful actions, and (case3) sequences with the meaningful actions excluded; sorting actions were excluded from consideration in “Club Membership” due to infrequency.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 Problem Solving (Party Invitation log actions)
main_findings.target_variable: Party Invitation performance group (score0 vs score3)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Doc2Vec + Neural Network: F1 0.850–0.962 and accuracy 0.850–0.946 across cases; best case2 (mail-moving actions only) accuracy 94.6% with silhouette 0.491. Doc2Vec + Random Forest: F1 0.893–0.951 and accuracy 0.852–0.930 across cases; best case2 accuracy 92.3% with similar silhouette improvement.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 Problem Solving data from the “Party Invitation” problem set, the study leveraged embedded action-sequence representations (Word2Vec/Doc2Vec) and focused on mail-moving actions to predict the performance group (score0 vs score3), finding that restricting to the meaningful mail-moving actions (case2) produced the highest clustering coherence (silhouette 0.491) and the strongest classification performance (NN accuracy 94.6%, F1 up to 0.962). This indicates that identifying and validating a small set of high-impact actions can improve automated detection of low vs high problem-solving performance from log data, supporting adaptive feedback systems that target the specific action steps learners miss, though the results are based on log-derived group labels and do not establish causal effects.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC 2012 Problem Solving (Club Membership log actions)
main_findings.target_variable: Club Membership performance group (correct vs incorrect)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Doc2Vec + Neural Network: F1 0.862–0.917 and accuracy 0.862–0.876 across cases; best case2 (mail-sending + environment actions) F1 0.917 and accuracy 0.876 with silhouette 0.333. Doc2Vec + Random Forest: F1 0.761–0.923 and accuracy 0.652–0.930 across cases; best case2 accuracy 0.880 and F1 0.923.
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC 2012 Problem Solving data from the “Club Membership” problem set, the study leveraged embedded action-sequence representations and selected mail-sending plus environment actions as meaningful steps to predict the performance group (correct vs incorrect), finding that case2 increased separation (silhouette 0.333) and improved classification (NN F1 up to 0.917, accuracy 0.876; RF accuracy up to 0.880). This indicates that log-based action-step identification can yield compact, interpretable behavioral signals for distinguishing correct from incorrect task completion, informing targeted instructional or system feedback that emphasizes the critical action steps, while generalization may be limited by the single-dataset context and the absence of explicit survey-weighted inference.

data.outcome_summary: The study analyzes 2012 PIAAC problem-solving log data for two tasks (“Party Invitation” with 35 actions; “Club Membership” with 25 actions) and preprocesses logs by removing incomplete sequences with missing actions. It converts action sequences into embeddings using Word2Vec (action-level) and Doc2Vec (sequence-level), then validates “meaningful actions” via clustering coherence (silhouette scores) and supervised group classification using a neural network and random forest. For “Party Invitation,” focusing on mail-moving actions (case2) yields the best separation (silhouette 0.491) and the strongest NN performance (accuracy 94.6%, F1 up to 0.962). For “Club Membership,” focusing on mail-sending and environment actions (case2) improves separation (silhouette 0.333) and classification (NN F1 up to 0.917, accuracy 0.876; RF accuracy up to 0.880). Limitations include lack of explicit survey-weight handling discussion, reliance on log-derived group labels, and potential representativeness constraints.
